summary: This October 3, 2023 article argues that local wetlands, once dismissed as wastelands, are vital for water quality, flood control, the economy, biodiversity and climate regulation. It cites studies and reports with figures on nutrient removal, floodwater storage, fishing revenue, ecotourism, species counts and carbon sequestration. It also covers threats, the Wetland Preservation Act, community and school initiatives, and future monitoring with drones and satellites.
one_line: Local wetlands deliver water purification, flood control, economic value, biodiversity and carbon storage, and are now being protected through new policy, community action and education.
key_facts: A study commissioned by the local Environmental Research Institute on September 15, 2023 found nearby marshes removed an estimated 75% of incoming nitrogen loads and nearly 50% of phosphorus.
Hydrologist Dr. Samuel Vincent's report, publicized September 28, said local wetlands can store approximately 1.5 million cubic meters of floodwater.
Fishery United's October 1 economic assessment said the local fishing industry, reliant on healthy wetlands, contributes upwards of $20 million annually.
The Department of Wildlife and Ecotourism estimates bird-watching in the wetlands draws over 10,000 visitors annually, worth roughly $300,000 in local revenue.
Biologist Dr. Rebecca Lin's field study, published September 20, found over 200 bird species and 20 mammal species in the local wetlands, plus many amphibians, fish and invertebrates.
Dr. Lin reported a thriving population of spotted salamanders in the local marshlands; the species depends on water bodies for reproduction.
Peatlands cover only 3% of the globe's land surface but store more carbon than all other vegetation types combined.
A survey by the Global Wetlands and Climate Research Center, published October 10, estimated local peat bogs sequester approximately 5,000 tonnes of CO2 annually.
The Wetland Preservation Act, passed September 30, aims to protect and restore local wetlands; conservationist Maria Thompson is leading mapping and monitoring efforts.
Zoning laws have been updated to include wetland buffers that restrict construction that could destroy habitat.

Jenna Walters, head of the community organization 'Wetlands for Tomorrow', reports exponential growth in community-led clean-up and restoration projects since the awareness campaign launched in late September.
Educator Mark Breiner has run 'Wetland Warriors' workshops in local schools since September 1.
Researchers are using drone surveillance and satellite imagery to track changes in wetland coverage and health.
Wetlands face threats from urbanization, pollution, invasive species, unsustainable agricultural practices and climate change.
